claim: Network-based modelling of brain connectivity interacts strongly with the shape and exact location of brain regions.
source: Previously we showed that network-based modelling of brain connectivity interacts strongly with the shape and exact location of brain regions, such that cross-subject variations in the spatial configuration of functional brain regions are being interpreted as changes in functional connectivity (Bijsterbosch et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Bijsterbosch et al., 2018).

claim: Cross-subject variations in the spatial configuration of functional brain regions are being interpreted as changes in functional connectivity.
source: Previously we showed that network-based modelling of brain connectivity interacts strongly with the shape and exact location of brain regions, such that cross-subject variations in the spatial configuration of functional brain regions are being interpreted as changes in functional connectivity (Bijsterbosch et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Bijsterbosch et al., 2018).

claim: Spatial effects on connectivity estimates occur as a result of spatial overlap between brain networks.
source: Here we show that these spatial effects on connectivity estimates actually occur as a result of spatial overlap between brain networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by data and analyses presented in the manuscript, including simulations and real data analyses.

claim: Spatial overlap between brain networks systematically biases connectivity estimates obtained from group spatial ICA followed by dual regression.
source: This is shown to systematically bias connectivity estimates obtained from group spatial ICA followed by dual regression.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical derivations, simulations, and empirical data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Distributed networks of brain regions exhibit coordinated activity of neural populations both within and between networks.
source: Distributed networks of brain regions exhibit coordinated activity of neural populations both within and between networks, known as functional connectivity (Fox et al., 2005; Greicius et al., 2003; Raichle et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature (Fox et al., 2005; Greicius et al., 2003; Raichle et al., 2001).

claim: Resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rfMRI) can be used to characterise the rich intrinsic functional organisation of the brain.
source: Resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rfMRI) can be used to characterise the rich intrinsic functional organisation of the brain (Biswal et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to foundational work (Biswal et al., 1995) and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Interindividual variability in estimated functional connectivity between brain regions is, to a large extent, driven by variability in the spatial organisation of large-scale brain networks.
source: We previously showed that interindividual variability in estimated functional connectivity between brain regions is, to a large extent, driven by variability in the spatial organisation (i.e., the precise shape and location) of large-scale brain networks (Bijsterbosch et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Bijsterbosch et al., 2018).

claim: Spatial information explained up to 62% of interindividual variance in node-based functional connectivity.
source: Specifically, our previous results revealed that node-based functional connectivity as normally estimated from rfMRI data is influenced by a mixture of spatial and temporal factors, with spatial information explaining up to 62% of interindividual variance.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative results from previous work.

claim: Cross-subject variability in spatial organisation strongly influenced node-based functional connectivity estimates regardless of the parcellation type/method.
source: We found that the cross-subject variability in spatial organisation strongly influenced node-based functional connectivity estimates regardless of the parcellation type/method (Bijsterbosch et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Bijsterbosch et al., 2018) that tested multiple parcellation methods.

claim: Cortical alignment using 'MSMAll' incorporates multiple spatial features including folding patterns, myelin maps, functional resting state networks, and visuotopic maps for alignment.
source: Cortical alignment using 'MSMSulc' is driven by gyral folding patterns alone, whereas cortical alignment using 'MSMAll' incorporates multiple spatial features including folding patterns, myelin maps, functional resting state networks, and visuotopic maps for alignment.
evidence: This claim describes established methods for cortical alignment.

claim: MSMAll shows substantial improvements in alignment compared with MSMSulc.
source: Previous work has shown substantial improvements in alignment when using MSMAll compared with MSMSulc, and both types of surface alignment are superior compared with volumetric alignment (Coalson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Coalson et al., 2018).

claim: Both types of surface alignment (MSMAll and MSMSulc) are superior compared with volumetric alignment.
source: Previous work has shown substantial improvements in alignment when using MSMAll compared with MSMSulc, and both types of surface alignment are superior compared with volumetric alignment (Coalson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Coalson et al., 2018).

claim: Correlation between group ICA maps and individual-subject ICA maps is highest for MSMAll and lowest for volumetric data.
source: The main effect was significant (F(2,1098)=673.2, p<10−10), and all post-hoc paired tests were significant after Bonferroni correction (MSMAll-MSMSulc ΔZ=0.045, p<10−10; MSMSulc-volumetric ΔZ=0.152, p<10−10; see Figure 1, Figure 1—figure Supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data comparing different alignment methods, with results shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure Supplement 1A.

claim: Dual regression was largely able to overcome misalignment between MSMSulc subject data and MSMAll group maps to estimate the subject-specific spatial organisation.
source: These results show that, despite misalignment between MSMSulc subject data and MSMAll group maps, dual regression was largely able to overcome this misalignment to estimate the subject-specific spatial organisation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis comparing dual regression results across different alignment methods.

claim: Dual regression was not able to correct for the more substantial amounts of misalignment observed in volumetrically aligned data.
source: However, dual regression was not able to correct for the more substantial amounts of misalignment observed in volumetrically aligned data.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis showing lower correlations for volumetric data.

claim: The difference in correlation between dual regression and ground truth maps between MSMAll and MSMSulc did not reach significance (ΔZ=0.013, p=0.061).
source: Conversely, the difference in this correlation between MSMAll and MSMSulc did not reach significance (ΔZ=0.013, p=0.061; see Figure 1, Figure 1—figure Supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis with specific p-value and effect size reported.

claim: There is a significant negative correlation between ICA-DR temporal network matrix edges and ICA-DR spatial overlap matrix edges across edges and subjects.
source: The results reveal a significant negative correlation (across edges and subjects) between ICA-DR temporal network matrix edges and ICA-DR spatial overlap matrix edges (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: When the spatial maps for two nodes are less correlated, there is more positive functional connectivity between these nodes.
source: This means that when the spatial maps for two nodes are less correlated (e.g. there is less spatial overlap), then there is more positive functional connectivity between these nodes.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the negative correlation observed in the data.

claim: Thresholding can be used in the presence of noise to recover spatial overlap between group spatial ICA node maps.
source: Previous work has shown that thresholding can be used in the presence of noise to recover spatial overlap between group spatial ICA node maps (Beckmann et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Beckmann et al., 2005).

claim: Spatial ICA leads to an underestimation of map weights in the overlapping area.
source: Example group maps estimated using spatial ICA show somewhat weaker weights in the overlapping region, consistent with the independence constraint (Figure 4A and insert).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Temporal network matrix edges estimated with dual regression were shifted positively compared to the ground truth.
source: As expected, the temporal network matrix edges were shifted positively compared to the ground truth (Figure 4C), and the spatial overlap matrix edges were shifted negatively compared to the ground truth (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Spatial overlap matrix edges estimated with dual regression were shifted negatively compared to the ground truth.
source: As expected, the temporal network matrix edges were shifted positively compared to the ground truth (Figure 4C), and the spatial overlap matrix edges were shifted negatively compared to the ground truth (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Individual maps and timecourses estimated with ICA-DR are highly correlated with the ground truth.
source: Nevertheless, the individual maps and timecourses estimated with ICA-DR are highly correlated with the ground truth (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Even though first-order map and timecourse estimates from ICA-DR may have good accuracy, second-order spatial and temporal edge estimates can be more strongly affected by systematic shifts if the assumption of spatial independence is not met.
source: Hence, even though the first-order map and timecourse estimates from ICA-DR may have good accuracy, second-order spatial and temporal edge estimates can be more strongly affected by systematic shifts if the assumption of spatial independence is not met.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results showing high accuracy for maps/timecourses but biased edge estimates.

claim: Spatial overlap occurs most noticeably in the temporal-parietal-occipital junction.
source: The absolute sum across node maps reveals a cortical pattern of overlap regions. Overlap occurs most noticeably in the temporal-parietal-occipital junction, and the spatial organisation is similar between PROFUMO results (left) and ICA-DR results (right).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The spatial organisation of overlap is similar between PROFUMO results and ICA-DR results.
source: Overlap occurs most noticeably in the temporal-parietal-occipital junction, and the spatial organisation is similar between PROFUMO results (left) and ICA-DR results (right).
evidence: This claim is supported by visual comparison in Figure 5A.

claim: Overlap is somewhat more extensive in PROFUMO results compared with ICA-DR.
source: As expected, overlap is somewhat more extensive in PROFUMO results compared with ICA-DR.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and is consistent with theoretical expectations.

claim: The spatial correlation between un-thresholded PFM maps is strong (r = 0.46), whereas there is no correlation between the two un-thresholded ICA maps.
source: However, the spatial correlation between the two un-thresholded PFM maps is strong (r = 0.46), whereas there is no correlation between the two un-thresholded ICA maps.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative correlation analysis of specific map pairs.

claim: The accuracy of estimated timeseries is relatively good in all of the analysis pipelines tested (PROFUMO, traditional ICA-DR, and thresholded ICA-DR).
source: The results show that the accuracy of estimated timeseries is relatively good in all of the analysis pipelines tested here (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The accuracy of spatial map estimation is superior in PROFUMO compared to both variations of the ICA-DR pipeline.
source: The accuracy of spatial map estimation is superior in PROFUMO compared to both variations of the ICA-DR pipeline (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The accuracy of spatial map estimates was improved using the thresholded ICA-DR pipeline compared to the traditional ICA-DR pipeline.
source: As expected, the accuracy of spatial map estimates was improved using the thresholded ICA-DR pipeline compared to the traditional ICA-DR pipeline (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: For edges with significantly positive ground truth spatial correlation, PROFUMO outperformed both ICA-DR pipelines for estimating spatial edges.
source: When focusing on edges with significantly positive ground truth spatial correlation, PROFUMO outperformed both ICA-DR pipelines for estimating spatial edges (Figure 7E), whereas thresholded ICA-DR results were closest to the ground truth for estimating temporal edges (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7E.

claim: For edges with significantly positive ground truth spatial correlation, thresholded ICA-DR results were closest to the ground truth for estimating temporal edges.
source: When focusing on edges with significantly positive ground truth spatial correlation, PROFUMO outperformed both ICA-DR pipelines for estimating spatial edges (Figure 7E), whereas thresholded ICA-DR results were closest to the ground truth for estimating temporal edges (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The strongest relationship with behaviour is observed for spatial overlap matrices estimated with PROFUMO (RUV = 0.72).
source: The strongest relationship with behaviour is observed for spatial overlap matrices estimated with PROFUMO (RUV = 0.72), which is significantly stronger than with the original ICA-DR temporal network matrix result (p=0.03), and compared with the thresholded ICA-DR temporal network matrix result (p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by CCA analysis with statistical significance testing.

claim: PROFUMO spatial overlap matrices show significantly stronger relationship with behaviour than original ICA-DR temporal network matrices (p=0.03).
source: The strongest relationship with behaviour is observed for spatial overlap matrices estimated with PROFUMO (RUV = 0.72), which is significantly stronger than with the original ICA-DR temporal network matrix result (p=0.03), and compared with the thresholded ICA-DR temporal network matrix result (p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of CCA results.

claim: PROFUMO spatial overlap matrices show significantly stronger relationship with behaviour than thresholded ICA-DR temporal network matrices (p=0.001).
source: The strongest relationship with behaviour is observed for spatial overlap matrices estimated with PROFUMO (RUV = 0.72), which is significantly stronger than with the original ICA-DR temporal network matrix result (p=0.03), and compared with the thresholded ICA-DR temporal network matrix result (p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of CCA results.

claim: The amount of overall shared variance between temporal network and spatial overlap matrices was 29.6% for original ICA-DR, 26.8% for thresholded ICA-DR, and 24.5% for PROFUMO.
source: Specifically, the amount of overall shared variance between temporal network and spatial overlap matrices was 29.6% for original ICA-DR, 26.8% for thresholded ICA-DR, and 24.5% for PROFUMO.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of shared variance.

claim: Both thresholded ICA-DR and PROFUMO show reduced conflation of temporal and spatial information compared with traditional ICA-DR.
source: Hence, these results show reduced conflation of temporal and spatial information in both thresholded ICA-DR and PROFUMO compared with traditional ICA-DR.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the shared variance analysis showing lower percentages for thresholded ICA-DR and PROFUMO.

claim: The partial CCA result for the ICA-DR thresholded temporal network matrix was no longer significantly linked to the positive-negative behavioural mode (Rpartial = 0.01, pBonferroni = 1).
source: Interestingly, the partial CCA result for the ICA-DR thresholded temporal network matrix was no longer significantly linked to the positive-negative behavioural mode (Rpartial = 0.01, pBonferroni = 1), supporting the interpretation that cross-subject behavioural variability in temporal network matrices is largely driven by spatial information.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of partial CCA results.

claim: Cross-subject behavioural variability in temporal network matrices is largely driven by spatial information.
source: Interestingly, the partial CCA result for the ICA-DR thresholded temporal network matrix was no longer significantly linked to the positive-negative behavioural mode (Rpartial = 0.01, pBonferroni = 1), supporting the interpretation that cross-subject behavioural variability in temporal network matrices is largely driven by spatial information.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the loss of significance in partial CCA after removing spatial information.

claim: Functional networks are often spatially overlapping.
source: Our results reveal that functional networks are often spatially overlapping (Figure 5), and that individual differences in the amount of spatial overlap (and resulting spatial correlation) is likely to explain our previous results.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Individual differences in the amount of spatial overlap is likely to explain previous results showing conflation of temporal and spatial information.
source: Our results reveal that functional networks are often spatially overlapping (Figure 5), and that individual differences in the amount of spatial overlap (and resulting spatial correlation) is likely to explain our previous results.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings about spatial overlap and its effects on connectivity estimates.

claim: Spatial overlap is underestimated in spatial ICA due to the statistical independence constraint.
source: These findings support the main results from our earlier article that estimated temporal correlations are (in part) driven by spatial information (Bijsterbosch et al., 2018). However, our new findings show that these results should not be interpreted as spatial misalignment (as we suggested in our earlier work), but are rather the result of spatially overlapping functional organization. Spatial overlap is underestimated in spatial ICA (due to the statistical independence constraint; Figure 4A), systematically affecting downstream dual regression steps, such that the resulting temporal network matrices are negatively weighted by any spatial correlations present in the underlying true networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical theory and simulation results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Temporal network matrices from dual regression are negatively weighted by any spatial correlations present in the underlying true networks.
source: Spatial overlap is underestimated in spatial ICA (due to the statistical independence constraint; Figure 4A), systematically affecting downstream dual regression steps, such that the resulting temporal network matrices are negatively weighted by any spatial correlations present in the underlying true networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical derivations and simulation results.

claim: Patterns of spatial overlap may be highly sensitive to individual differences in behaviour.
source: Secondly, our findings suggest that patterns of spatial overlap may be highly sensitive to individual differences in behaviour and warrant further research.
evidence: This claim is supported by the strong CCA results for spatial overlap matrices.

claim: Dual regression obtains relatively accurate estimates in the presence of minor misalignment when using surface-based alignment methods.
source: The results in Figure 1 reveal that dual regression obtains relatively accurate estimates in the presence of minor misalignment (as modelled with MSMAll compared with MSMSulc), suggesting that spatial misalignment may not contribute strongly when care is taken to adopt surface-based alignment methods and subject-specific node-definition approaches.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis comparing different alignment methods shown in Figure 1.

claim: Misalignment is likely to play a larger role when using volume-based alignment procedures.
source: However, dual regression was not able to account for more extensive misalignment which is seen when using volume-based alignment procedures (Coalson et al., 2018). Therefore, it is likely that misalignment may influence functional connectivity estimates for analyses performed in volumetric space (Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed poor performance of dual regression with volumetric data and citation to previous work.

claim: Misalignment is likely to play a larger role when using anatomically-derived hard parcellations that are unlikely to match the subject-specific functional organisation well.
source: Similarly, misalignment is likely to play a larger role when using anatomically-derived hard parcellations that are unlikely to match the subject-specific functional organisation well.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the understanding of how hard parcellations work.

claim: The correct interpretation of spatial edges is an important new research question that requires further investigation.
source: However, the correct interpretation of spatial edges is an important new research question that requires further investigation.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future research.

claim: Thresholded dual regression will be implemented in the next version of FSL dual_regression.
source: Thresholded dual regression will be implemented in the next version of FSL dual_regression (https://fsl.fmrib.ox.ac.uk/fsl/fslwiki/DualRegression).
evidence: This is a statement about future software implementation.

claim: Spatial correlations obtained from PROFUMO are most strongly linked to behaviour.
source: Our results show that spatial correlations obtained from PROFUMO are most strongly linked to behaviour (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by CCA analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Cross-subject variance in spatial correlations are behaviourally-relevant.
source: Hence, this result indicates that cross-subject variance in spatial correlations (rather than in more complex aspects of spatial organisation) are behaviourally-relevant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CCA results showing strong associations for spatial overlap matrices.

claim: PROFUMO outperforms thresholded dual regression in the accuracy of estimated spatial maps and correlations.
source: Unfortunately, spatial correlations obtained from thresholded dual regression are not as strongly associated with behaviour (Figure 8), which is likely linked to the fact that PROFUMO outperforms thresholded dual regression in the accuracy of estimated spatial maps and correlations (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Spatial overlap was prominent in the temporo-parietal-occipital junction and within higher visual areas along the lateral wall.
source: Our findings show that spatial overlap was prominent in the temporo-parietal-occipital junction and within higher visual areas along the lateral wall (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The hierarchical functional organisation of V1 represents overlapping receptive fields with selectivity for stimulus orientation, length, width, or colour.
source: The hierarchical functional organisation of V1 is relatively well-understood to represent overlapping receptive fields with selectivity for stimulus orientation, length, width, or colour (Van Essen and Maunsell, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established neuroscience literature.

claim: Data from the Human Connectome Project S1200 release were used including 1004 subjects with 4800 resting state timepoints.
source: Data from the Human Connectome Project S1200 release were used including 1004 subjects with 4800 resting state timepoints (Van Essen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the dataset used in the study.

claim: The data were preprocessed using the HCP minimally preprocessing pipeline.
source: The data were preprocessed using the HCP minimally preprocessing pipeline (Glasser et al., 2013), followed by FIX cleanup of artificial components obtained from single-run ICA (Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the preprocessing methods used, supported by citations.

claim: Three subjects were excluded for CCA purposes due to incomplete genetic information.
source: Three subjects were excluded for CCA purposes due to incomplete genetic information (i.e., N = 1001 for CCA).
evidence: This describes a data exclusion criterion.
